faq.q: Why do starfish drop their arms?
faq.a: Dropping an arm, called autotomy, lets a starfish escape when a predator grabs it. The arm breaks off at a weak point, the wound seals, and a new arm begins to grow.
asks: Can a starfish lose an arm on purpose?

faq.q: What is inside a starfish's arm?
faq.a: Each arm has digestive glands, part of the nerve ring that runs around the body, rows of tube feet worked by water pressure, and in adults, parts that make eggs or sperm.

faq.q: How do starfish cells rebuild an arm?
faq.a: Cells near the wound change into flexible, stem-like cells that divide and build all the tissues the arm needs. A tiny new arm appears and grows slowly to full size.
asks: How does a new starfish arm grow?

faq.q: How long does a starfish take to regrow an arm?
faq.a: It is slow: usually months, and up to a year or more for a full-size arm. Regrowing costs a lot of energy, so the starfish may grow or breed less in the meantime.
asks: Does regrowing an arm cost energy?

faq.q: Can a starfish arm grow a whole new starfish?
faq.a: In most species an arm needs part of the central disc to regrow a whole body. A few, such as the blue Linckia sea star, can grow an entire new animal from a single arm, a form nicknamed a comet.
asks: Can you cut a starfish in half to make two?

facts: Starfish are echinoderms, related to sea urchins, not fish; many scientists call them sea stars.
Some sea stars, such as Linckia, can regenerate a whole body from a single severed arm.
